content: A microbial pest control agent (MPCA) refers to a microorganism that serves as the active substance in pest control. This includes bacteria, fungi, protozoa, viruses, or other microscopic self-replicating entities, along with any associated metabolites responsible for pest control effects. These microorganisms may be viable (capable of replication) or non-viable (unable to replicate or transfer genetic material). The metabolites or toxins produced during microbial growth, as well as materials from the growth medium, are included as long as they have not been intentionally altered. A microbial pest control product (MPCP) is a product containing an MPCA that is registered or labeled with specific instructions for direct use in pest control. The technical grade of an MPCA refers to the purest preparation of the microbial material obtained from the production process, containing no additives except those necessary for microbial growth or purification. This material may be distributed to manufacturers in its pure form or with stabilizers, preservatives, or diluents. Pathogenicity is the ability of a microorganism to cause disease or damage to a host. Pathogens may cause disease through a combination of toxicity and invasiveness or colonization. In some cases, disease results from an abnormal reaction of the host’s defense system. Secondary compounds (metabolites) are non-essential microbial products that may be of toxicological concern to human or animal health or the environment. Symbiosis describes a mutually beneficial interaction between two organisms living in close association. Mycotoxins are toxins produced by fungi, while viroids are infectious agents consisting of small RNA strands that do not code for proteins but replicate using host cell enzymes. Viroids are known to cause several diseases. The registration of microbial pesticides requires specific data and information to evaluate their safety and efficacy. These requirements are adapted from those used for chemical pesticides but are tailored to the unique nature of microbial products. Regulatory authorities may need specialized training to evaluate MPCAs and MPCPs properly. In some cases, testing may be conducted on the final product (MPCP) rather than the active substance (MPCA) due to the enclosed nature of the production process. Biological properties such as the origin, ecology, life cycle, and potential to produce toxic secondary compounds must also be provided. For human health assessments, data on the pathogenic potential, infectivity, and clearance of the microorganism, as well as toxicological effects of secondary metabolites, are required. Higher-tier studies may be needed if adverse effects are observed. Sensitization testing is generally not required unless secondary metabolites are present. Genotoxicity data is required if relevant secondary compounds are identified. Residue studies are typically not required for MPCAs approved for crop protection and public health, as these microorganisms are not human pathogens. Environmental assessments depend on whether the MPCA is indigenous or non-indigenous. For indigenous species, data may be waived if the release levels are similar to natural occurrences and no relevant secondary compounds are present. For non-indigenous species, additional studies on environmental persistence and effects on non-target organisms may be required. Methodologies may need to be adapted for these assessments. Ecotoxicological data is required to evaluate the effects of MPCAs and MPCPs on non-target organisms. For insect-pathogenic MPCAs, information on pathogenicity to bees and other relevant organisms must be provided. Efficacy data from high-quality field trials is necessary to demonstrate the product’s effectiveness under labeled conditions. Data from laboratory or growth chamber studies may supplement field trials, and extrapolation between crops for the same target pest may be acceptable. In summary, the evaluation of microbial pest control agents and products requires a comprehensive understanding of their biological, toxicological, and ecological properties.
